# mibz2

> A bzip2 decoder built for memory-level parallelism.

mibz2 is a bzip2 decoder, block-parallel, its inverse BWT walked as interleaved chains
within each block, with byte-for-byte libbzip2 output and every block and stream CRC
checked, from Python (`mibz2.decompress`, `mibz2.open`) or Rust (`mibz2::decode`,
`mibz2::BzReader`). Install with `pip install mibz2` or `cargo add mibz2`. Each link below
is the Markdown version of a page of https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/.

# Benchmarks

# Benchmarks

mibz2's speed is measured on GitHub's runners by the Benchmark workflow (`.github/workflows/bench.yml`), with the A/B harness `examples/ab.rs` and `bench/report.py`. Nothing about performance is decided on a developer's machine.

- [History](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/history/index.md>): master's figures over its commits.
- [Alternatives](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/alternatives/index.md>): the latest master commit against the other bzip2 decoders: pbz2, lbzip2, indexed\_bzip2, fbz, the `lbzip2` crate, libbzip2 and libbz2-rs.

These are decoder-level results: one process decoding one file, nothing else. End-to-end results, the decoder inside a pipeline, are in [wikidata-pq's benchmark history](<https://lmmx.github.io/wikidata-pq/guide/bench-history/>).

## What runs when

| event | arms | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a pull request that touches the decoder, the harness, the corpora or the bench | its head and its base (the merge base with master), both built on the runner | one comment on the pull request, edited in place on every push |
| a push to master | mibz2 and the [alternatives](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/alternatives/index.md>) | the commit's result on the `bench-results` branch, and these pages |
| the Actions tab | either: a base commit given, as a pull request; none, as master | the run's summary, not recorded |

Pull requests never run the alternatives: their runs are the head against the base only. The alternatives that are Rust crates with dependencies of their own (fbz, the `lbzip2` crate, libbz2-rs) are built into a second build of the harness, `bench/alternatives`, so the crate's own dev-dependencies stay as they are.

Only master's commits are recorded. A pull request's runs, and experiments that did not land, are not recorded or shown here; experiments are written up in the [journals](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/background/journals/index.md>).

## The workload

- **The crate's corpora** (`ab gen`, `tests/common/mod.rs`), at scale 4, each compressed by libbzip2 1.0.8 at level 9: `text` (the crate's own sources and README, repeated: 12 MB), `random` (8 MB), `onebyte` (one byte repeated, 20 MB), `pattern` (a 7-byte pattern, 19.6 MB), `runs` (runs of random lengths, 10 MB) and `records` (binary records, 9.6 MB). The `text` corpus is made from the commit's own sources, so its bytes change a little from commit to commit.
- **The Wikidata dump's own blocks:** 12 byte-range windows of 1 MiB of `wikidata-20261019-all.json.bz2`, at (2i + 1)/24 of the file. `examples/windows.rs` keeps each window's whole blocks, their bits untouched, as a stream of its own, checked against libbzip2 and lbzip2: 431 blocks, 11.85 MB of bz2 → 209.7 MB of JSON (17.69×). `bench/wikidata.json` pins each window's offset, length and SHA-256, and the corpus's. Wikimedia serves a dated dump for about six weeks, so the windows are kept on the repository's `bench-data` branch.

## How it is measured

- **A run** is one process decoding one file from disk, end to end, its output hashed (the same hash for every arm, or the run fails: the same-bytes check). It records the wall time, the CPU time (user + sys), the peak RSS, and each thread's CPU.
- **A round** decodes every corpus once with each arm at each thread count: 1 thread (pinned to one CPU) and the runner's cores. The arms' order is rotated and reversed round to round. There are 10 rounds.
- **Block-parallel or single-threaded:** each arm is classed in its records (`parallel`). A single-threaded decoder (libbzip2, libbz2-rs) runs at 1 thread only, once a round; at the runner's cores its figures are those 1-thread runs, paired with mibz2's at that count, and shown as 1-thread runs, never as a decode on more threads.
- **On a pull request**, the base's own harness binary is an arm (`mibz2@base/ab`), so both builds run in the same process shape on the same runner.
- **Paired ratios:** each round's ratio of one arm's time to the reference arm's (the base; or mibz2, against the alternatives), their geometric mean, and its 95% t-interval over the rounds. A change is called faster or slower only where the interval excludes no change.
- **The bench version** (`bench/report.py`, semver) is stamped on every result. A change to what is measured or how is a new major version, and the history never joins a series across major versions, runner CPU models or sets of corpora.

## The full-dump figure is modelled

Each result also gives a whole dump's decode (103.5 GB of bz2), **modelled, not measured**, from the Wikidata blocks' runs, round by round:

- the scanner's time (the one serial thread: each block's header and Huffman symbols) per byte of bz2, scaled by the dump's bz2 bytes;
- the workers' time per byte of output, scaled by the dump's output, taken as its bz2 bytes times the sample's ratio (17.69×; another sample of the same dump, 24 windows of 25 MB, measured 18.68×; wikidata-pq's CI slice, lines recompressed, is 13.69×);
- at N threads, the larger of the scanner's time and the workers' over N, times the sample's own wall over that bound; the same gap read as a fixed cost is given beside it.

It assumes time linear in bytes, the sample's mix standing for the dump's, and the runner's CPU; its interval carries the rounds' spread and the sample ratio's.

# History

Loading the chart…

Master's mibz2 figures over its commits, oldest to newest. The chart above draws every figure at once; below it, one chart per corpus and thread count. Each point is a recorded commit (linked to it): the mean of its 10 rounds, and its 95% interval as a whisker. The figures are measured on GitHub's runners ([methodology](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/index.md>)).

- **Separate lines, never joined:** a line holds one runner CPU model and core count, one set of corpora, and one content of its corpus. Runners of one kind differ in speed from another (an AMD EPYC 7763 from a 9V45), so a commit measured on another kind of runner starts or joins that kind's line, in that kind's colour.
- **Joined only between neighbouring commits:** where commits measured on other runners come between two of a kind's points, its line breaks, so no segment spans commits it didn't measure. Its points either side still compare (same runner model, same corpus); they are different runs on possibly different hosts, not a paired comparison.
- **Bench versions:** a line runs on across bench versions that left these figures' meaning alone, and splits where a version redefined them ([the benchmark's changelog](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/bench/CHANGELOG.md>)). Each point's tooltip names the version that measured it.
- **`text`'s points stand alone:** that corpus is generated from mibz2's own sources, so its bytes change from commit to commit, and no two of its points are the same workload.
- **Trunk only:** pull requests and experiments are not recorded.
- **Peak RSS** is one of the figures (the selector above the charts).

These are decoder-level results. End-to-end results, the decoder in wikidata-pq's pipeline, are in [wikidata-pq's tracker](<https://lmmx.github.io/wikidata-pq/guide/bench-history/>).

# Alternatives

Loading the chart…

mibz2 beside other bzip2 decoders on master's latest recorded commit, decoded in the same rounds on one runner ([methodology](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/index.md>)). A ratio above 1× is the alternative taking longer (or more memory) than mibz2: there, mibz2 is faster. These are decoder-level results; end-to-end pipeline results are in [wikidata-pq's tracker](<https://lmmx.github.io/wikidata-pq/guide/bench-history/>).

| decoder | what runs | threads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| pbz2 | Soof Golan's Rust decoder: `DecoderReader`, or `ParallelDecoder::with_threads` | block-parallel |
| lbzip2 | the C program: `lbzip2 -dc -n T`, read through a pipe | block-parallel |
| indexed\_bzip2 | C++, from Python: `IndexedBzip2File(path, parallelization=T)` (`bench/ib.py`; the interpreter's start left out) | block-parallel |
| fbz | Answer.AI's Rust decoder: `fbz::Reader`, `threads: T` | block-parallel |
| lbzip2-rs | the `lbzip2` crate (pure Rust): `StreamingBz2Read`, on the CPUs it may run on (it takes no thread count) | block-parallel |
| libbzip2 | the reference C library, 1.0.8: the `bzip2` crate's bundled source, `MultiBzDecoder` (as `bzip2 -dc` and Python's `bz2` decode) | single-threaded |
| libbz2-rs | libbz2-rs-sys, the pure-Rust port of libbzip2, through the `bzip2` crate 0.6 | single-threaded |
| bz2ngrs | Softleif's safe-Rust port of bz2-ng, at a pinned commit: `DecompressReader` | single-threaded (one thread a stream) |
| bz2ng | bz2-ng's C, at a pinned commit: its `bzip2 -dc`, read through a pipe (the reference bz2ngrs ports) | single-threaded |

**Single-threaded decoders run at 1 thread only.** libbzip2, libbz2-rs, bz2ngrs and bz2ng have no thread count, so they never decode on 4 threads. At 4 threads, their figures are their 1-thread runs against mibz2's at 4 threads: in the chart, hollow points with dashed whiskers, under "single-threaded (1 thread)"; in the tables, marked ¹.

**mibz2's inverse BWT against bz2ngrs's and libsais's.** Below the decoders' tables, the kernels run on the same Wikidata blocks, with the build, the walk and the output's assembly timed apart where a kernel allows it. libsais 2.12.1 (Ilya Grebnov) is the fastest inverse BWT measured here. It is a library of BWT algorithms, not a bzip2 decoder, so it appears in that table only, never in the chart. Its build and walk happen inside one call, so it shows a total. bz2ngrs and mibz2 store the same successor link in each 32-bit entry, but a different byte beside it: bz2ngrs the row's first-column byte, mibz2 its last-column byte (lbzip2's packing). The table says which phase a whole-decoder difference comes from ([the study](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-29-bz2ngrs.md>)).

Not included: `bzip2 -dc` and Python's `bz2` module, which are libbzip2 itself (its arm stands for them); and bz2k, mibz2's own prototype, which it replaced.

The latest record: [`ae942bd`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/commit/ae942bdb135569224473116ffaa706f1c9e389ed>) (2026-10-30).

**mibz2 against pbz2, lbzip2, indexed\_bzip2, fbz, lbzip2-rs, libbzip2, libbz2-rs, bz2ngrs and bz2ng**: 10 rounds on one runner · [run](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/actions/runs/40988680203>)

AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor, 4 cores · rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13) · bench 3.2.0

Each round decodes every corpus once with each decoder at each thread count (`ab run`), their order rotated round to round. **Against mibz2** is the decoder's wall (or CPU, or peak RSS) over mibz2's: the geometric mean of the rounds' paired ratios and its 95% interval; above 1, mibz2 is faster (or leaner). 1-thread runs are pinned to one CPU.

Block-parallel: pbz2, lbzip2, indexed\_bzip2, fbz, lbzip2-rs. Single-threaded (¹): libbzip2, libbz2-rs, bz2ngrs, bz2ng, run at 1 thread only; at 4 threads their figures are their 1-thread runs, against mibz2's at 4 threads.

**Same bytes:** every run of every arm gave the same output hash on that corpus, with no error.

## Resources: CPU per byte and scaling, the `wikidata` corpus

**CPU per byte** is the process's CPU (every thread, user + sys) over the output. **Amplification** is that at N threads over the same build's at 1, paired by round: 1× is no extra CPU for the same bytes, and above it the work costs more as threads are added (stalls, sharing, synchronisation; CPU counts a thread stalled on memory as running). **Efficiency** is the speedup over N. **Run-queue** is the threads' mean count runnable but not running.

| threads: placement | mibz2 MB/s | mibz2 CPU ns/B | mibz2 amplification | mibz2 efficiency | lbzip2 amplification | pbz2 amplification |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1: pinned to CPU 1 | 278 | 3.60 | 1 | – | 1 | 1 |
| 2: CPUs 0,2, one a core | 424 | 3.93 | 1.09× (1.08–1.10) | 76% | 1.01× (1.01–1.02) | 1.03× (1.03–1.03) |
| 4: all 4 CPUs, sharing SMT siblings | 533 | 6.25 | 1.73× (1.71–1.75) | 48% | 1.21× (1.21–1.22) | 1.63× (1.61–1.65) |

**Best:** mibz2 at 4 threads (533 MB/s); lbzip2 at 4 threads (196 MB/s); pbz2 at 4 threads (303 MB/s).

Conditions: 4 CPUs on 2 physical cores (0,1 | 2,3); no CPU quota; the run-queue counter checked and counting; 2-thread runs on CPUs 0,2 (one CPU a core); 4-thread runs share cores' SMT siblings.

**How to read it, and what it cannot show**

\- \*\*The four comparisons the assessment reads,\*\* declared in bench/report.py (\`assessment\`): best against best (wall), CPU per byte at the most threads, amplification at each thread count, and peak RSS at the most threads. Each moves only where its 95% interval excludes no change. With no real change, about one run in five flags one by chance: a flag that matters reproduces on a re-run. - \*\*A trade-off is not a failure.\*\* Faster for more CPU or memory, or the reverse, is for the reviewer to weigh against the deployment; the report names it, and nothing here fails CI but the outputs and the accounting. - \*\*What it can't show:\*\* which shared resource a rise in amplification comes from (cache, memory bandwidth, SMT, the scanner's handoffs): no hardware counters are read. CI's runners have 2 physical cores, so it cannot show a knee past 2 (the workstation's is at 4-5 workers, \#39). The cores' L3 is shared with other tenants and its size unknown. - \*\*Run-queue wait\*\* (threads' mean count runnable, not running; schedstat): mibz2 1t 0.00, mibz2 2t 0.72, mibz2 4t 0.94, lbzip2 1t 0.09, lbzip2 2t 0.30, lbzip2 4t 0.56, pbz2 1t 0.00, pbz2 2t 0.35, pbz2 4t 0.39. A pinned 2-thread run has four threads (two workers, the scanner, the reader) on two CPUs, so some wait is its shape, not interference. - \*\*The per-thread split's unattributed CPU\*\* (the process's total that no sampled thread holds, sampled every 10 ms): mibz2 2t 7%, mibz2 4t 5%, lbzip2 2t 4%, lbzip2 4t 6%, pbz2 2t 4%, pbz2 4t 4%.

## Where mibz2's CPU goes: the Wikidata blocks at 4 threads (median CPU seconds)

| build | scanner (serial) | workers (summed) | the reading thread and the rest | unattributed | wall |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mibz2 | 0.11 | 1.10 | 0.02 | 0.07 | 0.394 |

Unattributed: the process's CPU that no sampled thread holds (threads ending between samples). Before bench 3.0.0 the sampler ran every 50 ms and left 0.1-0.35 s a run here; a base built before 3.0.0 still does, so its split and the model below undercount its workers against head's.

## Where a decode's time goes, stage by stage: the Wikidata blocks on one thread (median c/B)

Each of 5 rounds runs the build's `examples/phases.rs` once (bench/stages.py), pinned to one CPU: the file decoded in decode order, block by block, each stage timed as it runs with the library's own functions (each stage's fastest of 2 passes), summed over the blocks, in cycles a byte of output at the reported clock (3246 MHz). Diagnostic only: the decoder's own figures are the tables above. 5 runs, 1m09s of the run.

| stage | mibz2 c/B (median) | share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| scanner (headers, Huffman) | 1.22 | 11.0% |
| MTF + RLE2 | 2.27 | 20.5% |
| T-vector build | 2.11 | 19.1% |
| walk (the one each build uses) | 4.93 | 44.6% |
| of which: segment assembly | 0.18 | 1.6% |
| RLE1 | 0.28 | 2.5% |
| CRC | 0.26 | 2.3% |
| **total** | 11.07 |  |

The walk row is the stage, the same in every build; its implementation is each build's own, as its `phases` names it: mibz2, “walk, room (used)”.

## The inverse BWT alone: mibz2's kernel against bz2ngrs's and libsais's, phase by phase (median ns/B)

The kernels on the same Wikidata blocks' last columns, on one pinned CPU, 10 passes of the file in decode order, the kernels' order rotating (`kernels`, bench/alternatives: bz2ngrs's src/bwt.rs as it is, its steps timed apart; libsais 2.12.1's `libsais_unbwt_cyclic_ctx`, built single-threaded from its pinned source, timed as one call a block, its build and walk inside it). Every block's bytes are checked the same from every kernel, and its CRC, before the timed passes. mibz2's build and libsais take the byte counts from MTF; bz2ngrs's counts them itself, so its build row holds that count. A ratio above 1× is the other kernel taking longer than mibz2's. libsais is an inverse BWT, not a bzip2 decoder: it isn't in the decoders' figures above. Diagnostic only: the decoders' own figures are the tables above.

| phase | mibz2 | bz2ngrs | libsais | bz2ngrs / mibz2 | libsais / mibz2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| T-vector build | 0.676 | 1.347 | (in its total) | 1.99× (1.99–2.00) |  |
| walk | 1.525 | 2.624 | (in its total) | 1.72× (1.71–1.73) |  |
| segment assembly (mibz2) / gather (bz2ngrs) | 0.053 | 0.052 | (in its total) | 0.97× (0.96–0.98) |  |
| inverse BWT, total | 2.253 | 4.023 | 3.339 | 1.78× (1.77–1.79) | 1.48× (1.47–1.49) |

## Modelled, not measured: a whole dump

The decode of `wikidata-20261019-all.json.bz2` (103 GB of bz2; 1.83 TB of JSON at the sample's 17.69×), scaled from the Wikidata blocks' runs above, round by round (mean ± its 95% interval, the sample ratio's own uncertainty added in):

|  | mibz2 |
| --- | ---: |
| 1 thread | 1h50m ± 13m11s |
| 4 threads | 57m26s ± 8m04s |
| 4 threads, the sample's overlap gap as a fixed cost | 40m05s ± 5m38s |
| the scanner alone (its serial part) | 16m18s ± 26.3s |
| the workers alone, over 4 | 40m05s ± 5m38s |

At 4 threads the workers bound it. Per byte: the scanner 9.4 ns a byte of bz2, the workers 5.25 ns a byte of output at 4 threads (CPU, summed over them), 3.08 ns at 1 thread (wall, less the scanner's part); the scanner would bind from about 10 worker threads (mibz2).

**What the model assumes**

\- \*\*Linear in bytes:\*\* the scanner's time in the dump's bz2 bytes, the workers' in its output bytes. - \*\*The sample stands for the dump:\*\* 12 windows of 1 MiB at (2i + 1)/24 of the dump, 431 of its own blocks; their mix of entities and their ratio, 17.69× (the windows' 95% interval ±14.0%), stand for the whole dump's. Another sample of the same dump (wikidata-pq's bench/full, 24 windows of 25 MB) measured 18.68×; wikidata-pq's CI slice, lines recompressed, is 13.69×. - \*\*The wall at N threads\*\* is the larger of the scanner's time and the workers' time over N (the scanner is one thread; the workers run blocks in parallel), times the sample's own wall over that bound: its overlap and fill taken to grow with the work, which errs long. Read as a fixed cost instead, the same gap gives the third row. - \*\*The machine is this runner,\*\* reading the dump from page cache: no download, no disk, no other work. The output is hashed by the reading thread and discarded. - The uncertainty is the rounds' spread, with the sample ratio's added in quadrature to the part that scales with the output; not the runner's: another CPU model gives other figures.

**The corpora, the machine and the toolchain**

| corpus | bz2 bytes | output bytes | SHA-256 | source | |---|--:|--:|---|---| | \`wikidata\` | 11,854,933 | 209,700,196 | \`82f65ace0731962d…\` | wikidata-20261019-all.json.bz2: 12 windows' whole blocks (bench/wikidata.json) | | \`onebyte\` | 51 | 20,000,000 | \`22924f5b3187645f…\` | ab gen (tests/common/mod.rs corpora), libbzip2 -9 | | \`pattern\` | 1,116 | 19,600,000 | \`0f07e2a274b91896…\` | ab gen (tests/common/mod.rs corpora), libbzip2 -9 | | \`random\` | 7,097,921 | 8,000,000 | \`10d444e6204289af…\` | ab gen (tests/common/mod.rs corpora), libbzip2 -9 | | \`records\` | 9,587,840 | 9,600,000 | \`ff8b5f6ed3dd4445…\` | ab gen (tests/common/mod.rs corpora), libbzip2 -9 | | \`runs\` | 37,995 | 10,000,235 | \`af3be4d130faf312…\` | ab gen (tests/common/mod.rs corpora), libbzip2 -9 | | \`text\` | 1,626,321 | 12,192,200 | \`853b8fbf38a1ba8b…\` | ab gen (tests/common/mod.rs corpora), libbzip2 -9 | - CPU: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor, 4 cores, reported clock 3246.0 MHz (cycles a byte use it), flags avx2, bmi1, bmi2, pclmulqdq, sse4\_1, ssse3; kernel 7.0.0-1017-azure; image ubuntu24 20261026.354.1 - rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13); pbz2 0.2.0; lbzip2 version 2.5; indexed\_bzip2 1.7.0; fbz 0.1.13; lbzip2-rs 0.5.13 (the lbzip2 crate); libbzip2 1.0.8 (the bzip2 crate's bundled source); libbz2-rs 0.2.5 (libbz2-rs-sys, through the bzip2 crate); bz2ngrs 0.1.0 at 6a92590 (git); bz2ng bz2-ng 0.1.0 (C, its \`bzip2 -dc\`); libbzip2 (the corpora's encoder) 1.0.8 (the bzip2 crate's bundled source); libsais (the kernels' only) 2.12.1 at c284ba8 (C: -O3 -march=native, single-threaded; bench/libsais.sh) - bench 3.2.0 (bench/report.py), 10 rounds, threads 1, 2, 4

# Throughput–memory frontier

In 2001 Seward set the inverse BWT's space–time trade-off for one block: a smaller table (`indexF`, the byte recovered from the first column) costs more work a step than the merged one (`mergedTL`, the byte kept beside each link, the layout mibz2 uses). The question here is whether that trade-off still holds when several blocks decode at once and their tables share one L3 cache. A table that is slower for one block might be faster for the machine, if its smaller footprint keeps more blocks resident.

**Where it stands:** the mechanism is measured, and so is a first shift. On the i9 and the Wikidata corpus, the full decoder with cooperative teams dominates every worker count measured (4 to 20) on both throughput and peak RSS (series 3). Whether it also does at 1 to 3 workers, the low-memory end, is not yet measured.

| finding | status |
| --- | --- |
| Shared cache capacity bounds throughput: the knee sits at about 14.4 MB of live tables, 0.7 of the i9's 20 MB L3, at two block sizes | measured ([workstation journal §9](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-28-workstation-scaling.md>)) |
| The table is compressible: about 77% of a full block's rows are in 32-row translation groups | measured ([ψ census](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/issues/99>)) |
| Sharing a block's table between threads moves the full decoder's throughput–RSS frontier: every worker count from 4 to 20 is dominated by a team configuration | measured on one machine and workload, at 4 threads and above ([decoder journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-29-cooperative-decoder.md>), series 3) |
| A compact table can be navigated as fast, built directly from the last column | not shown |
| A compact table gives more throughput from less memory than the best 32-bit configuration, on one machine and workload | not shown |

## The two charts

Both are drawn from [`frontier.json`](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/assets/data/frontier.json>), the page's measured observations. Point at a mark, or Tab to it, for its values. Every value is also in the tables [below](<#what-is-measured-so-far>).

1. **Throughput against memory:** each configuration's measured throughput and peak RSS, with the ones nothing beats on both ringed and joined by their step. This is the frontier. It draws series 3, the only one with measured RSS: the workers (arm `mibz2`), fixed teams of 2 and of 3, and the policy (v0.2.0's default). Where one plan ran at several thread counts, its marks are noise around one configuration. No worker counts below 4 were measured, so it is not yet the whole frontier.
2. **Throughput against concurrent full blocks,** as live table memory (blocks live × 3.6 MB, computed): where a smaller table would overtake the 32-bit one, if it does, as more blocks are live. No compact table exists yet, so it shows today's table and the knee measured in the [workstation journal §9](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-28-workstation-scaling.md>): series 1's worker counts and series 3's workers and teams, a panel each, since they are different workloads. Series 2, the inversion, is a different level: it has its own small panel and axes, never the decoder's.

The charts are drawn here by JavaScript. The tables [below](<#what-is-measured-so-far>) give every value they show.

**The rules the charts keep:** - **One machine and one workload a chart.** An L3 effect on the i9 may appear at another concurrency, or not at all, on another CPU. - **Two kinds of memory, never mixed:** the live tables' bytes (computed: live full blocks × 900,000 rows × 4 bytes for today's table) and the process's peak RSS (measured). Peak RSS also counts the scanner's slots, the output and every worker's buffers: at 4 threads on CI it is about 74 MB, against 14.4 MB of tables. - **Two levels, never mixed:** the full decoder (a file to verified output) and the research harness's inversion (MTF, build and walk). The headline is the full decoder; the inversion shows the mechanism. - **Releases are the record.** Selected pull requests and research runs appear as labelled overlays. - **Only measurements.** Footprints of designs that don't exist yet, and models, stay in the text. - **The frontier is judged against the best alternative,** not a convenient one. A compact table at four blocks beating today's at four blocks is a step; the frontier moves only if it beats today's best configuration at any block count.

## What is measured so far

Three series exist, on the i9 (Intel i9-10900K, 10 cores, 20 MB L3). They are different runs at different levels, so they are separate series, never one line.

**1\. The full decoder, today's table, by worker count** (unpinned; the bench corpus's bytes recompressed with lbzip2 -9; [workstation journal §9](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-28-workstation-scaling.md>)):

| workers | live tables | MB/s | CPU-seconds |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2 | 7.2 MB | 707 |  |
| **4** | **14.4 MB** | **1026** | 0.834 |
| 6 | 21.6 MB | 889 |  |
| 8 | 28.8 MB | 698 |  |
| 10 | 36.0 MB | 645 | 2.921 |

Past 4 workers, more tables than the L3 holds make each block's work dearer: from 4 to 10 workers the CPU-seconds rise 3.5× and throughput falls. Peak RSS was not recorded in this run.

**2\. The inversion, production against cooperative teams** (every thread pinned; the research harness's MTF, build and walk; [coop journal §17.4](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/research/coop-fused/docs/journal/2026-10-28-cooperative-inversion.md>)):

| configuration | live tables | cores | MB/s | against p4 (paired) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| p4, production | 14.4 MB | 4 | 1206 | 1 |
| y3x3, cooperative | 10.8 MB | 9 | 1657 | 1.375 ±0.022 |
| y4x2, cooperative | 14.4 MB | 8 | 1725 | 1.439 ±0.020 |

A cooperative team shares one block's table among k cores, so N teams keep N tables live on N × k cores. - y3x3 runs faster than p4 from fewer live tables. p4 is production's best worker count on this machine in every scaling run (series 1). - So at this level, in throughput against live table bytes, sharing a table already does better than every production configuration measured. - **It is not yet a frontier result:** - it is the inversion, not the decoder; - it is pinned; - its memory axis is computed table bytes, not peak RSS; - it uses more cores (CPU-seconds are not yet measured).

**3\. The full decoder, workers against cooperative teams, with measured memory** (unpinned; the bench corpus, 209.7 MB decoded; 20 interleaved rounds; the [decoder journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-29-cooperative-decoder.md>) and its raw files). One point per distinct plan: where two arms ran the same plan (the policy at 8, 10 and 20 threads is 4 teams of 2 on this machine; 2 teams of 3 ran at both 6 and 8), the table gives the range of their medians, which is noise.

| plan | live tables | threads | MB/s | against p4 (paired, 95%) | peak RSS | CPU-s | nondominated |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | :---: |
| 4 workers (p4) | 14.4 MB | 4 | 1007 | 1 | 76 MB | 0.84 | no |
| 6 workers | 21.6 MB | 6 | 858 | 0.861 (0.842–0.881) | 102 MB | 1.45 | no |
| 8 workers | 28.8 MB | 8 | 674 | 0.693 (0.673–0.714) | 128 MB | 2.41 | no |
| 10 workers | 36.0 MB | 10 | 632 | 0.644 (0.621–0.668) | 152 MB | 2.97 | no |
| 20 workers | 72.0 MB | 20 | 471 | 0.479 (0.462–0.497) | 267 MB | 7.31 | no |
| 1 team of 3 | 3.6 MB | 3 | 530 | 0.540 (0.524–0.556) | 35 MB | 0.77 | **yes** |
| 2 teams of 2 | 7.2 MB | 4 | 891 | 0.904 (0.885–0.923) | 50 MB | 0.73 | no |
| 2 teams of 3 | 7.2 MB | 6 | 987–988 | 1.004–1.006 | 50 MB | 0.82 | **yes** |
| 3 teams of 2 (the policy at 6) | 10.8 MB | 6 | 1155–1189 | 1.166 (1.123–1.210) to 1.200 | 64 MB | 0.81–0.84 | no |
| 3 teams of 3 | 10.8 MB | 9 | 1234 | 1.264 (1.211–1.318) | 64 MB | 0.96 | **yes** |
| 4 teams of 2 (the policy at 8–20) | 14.4 MB | 8 | 1223–1256 | 1.243–1.274; at 20, 1.257 (1.197–1.320) | 77 MB | 1.02–1.04 | **yes**, by its best median |
| 5 teams of 2 | 18.0 MB | 10 | 1147 | 1.162 (1.121–1.204) | 91 MB | 1.36 | no |
| 6 teams of 3 | 21.6 MB | 18 | 1084 | 1.095 (1.060–1.132) | 105 MB | 2.16 | no |

Peak RSS is measured (the median run's, in decimal MB). Live tables are computed. The nondominated column compares medians on throughput (higher) and peak RSS (lower) within this series.

What it shows, and what it doesn't: - **Every worker count measured is dominated.** p4, the decoder's best worker count here, is beaten on both axes by 3 teams of 2 (the policy at 6 threads: 1.166× with its lower bound 1.123, at 64 MB against 76) and by 3 teams of 3. - **The nondominated set is all teams:** 1×3, 2×3, 3×3 and 4×2. Measured by medians, 4×2 stays on the set by its best repeat. Its throughput is tied with 3×3's within noise (their intervals overlap almost entirely), at 13 MB more RSS and about 6% more CPU. 3×3 is a lead for refining the policy, not yet a result. - **Not a whole-frontier result.** No worker counts below 4 were measured in this run. At 1 to 3 workers, today's decoder may still own the low-memory end: series 1 has 2 workers at 707 MB/s, but without RSS. Filling that in needs the same A/B at 1, 2 and 3 threads. - **One machine, one workload, one level (the full decoder).** Threads above 10 share physical cores with SMT siblings.

## What fills it in

- **The low-memory end on the i9:** the same A/B at 1, 2 and 3 threads, where today's workers and the smallest teams meet.
- **The CI benchmark's release runs** measure wall time, CPU and peak RSS at 1, 2 and 4 threads on every release, on GitHub's 4-vCPU runners. That is below the i9's knee, so it can't show a crossover, but it keeps a frontier for every release.
- **Compact tables** join when one exists: a 24-bit link-only table (\#79) first, then others if the census and the walk's costs justify them. They are judged against the cooperative decoder now, not against the workers.

The research behind this page: Seward's trade-off revisited, verbatim ([the researcher](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-29-frontier/seward-frontier-research.md>), [the coordinator](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-29-frontier/seward-frontier-coordinator.md>)), and the [literature study](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-29-literature-study.md>).

# Concepts

# Concepts

mibz2 decodes bzip2 as libbzip2 1.0.8 defines it, byte for byte, with every check libbzip2 makes, and decodes several blocks at once.

- [Why 32 couriers beat one](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/couriers/index.md>): memory-level parallelism, the decoder's premise. One courier waits at every stop to learn the next address; 32 couriers' waits overlap. The lanes, the prefetch, the per-step cost that binds next, and the measurements.
- [What is checked, and when](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/checks/index.md>): block CRCs, stream CRCs, what an error reports, and the four inputs mibz2 refuses where libbzip2 does not.
- [How it works](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/how-it-works/index.md>): the one sequential phase (the scanner), the workers, and the inverse BWT walked as 32 interleaved chains.
- [Prior work](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/prior-work/index.md>): libbzip2; Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi (DCC 2012); lbzip2 and pbzip2.

# Why 32 couriers beat one: understanding memory-level parallelism

Most of a bzip2 decode is one loop, the inverse Burrows–Wheeler transform's walk, and that loop spends most of its time waiting for memory. mibz2 doesn't make memory any faster. It keeps many of the walk's memory requests in flight at once, so the waits overlap. That is **memory-level parallelism** (MLP), and it is the library's basic premise.

This page explains it with couriers and a dispatcher, then gives the mechanism behind each part of the picture, and the measurements so far. [How it works](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/how-it-works/index.md>) has the threads around the walk, and [Prior work](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/prior-work/index.md>) the work it builds on.

## One courier, one chain

A motorcycle courier learns each delivery address only on arriving at the previous one: open the envelope, read the next address. The third destination can't be known before reaching the second. The bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next.

That is the ordinary inverse BWT:

- **The table.** After Huffman decoding and move-to-front, a block's last column becomes the T-vector: one 32-bit entry a row, holding the row's byte (bits 0–7) and the next row (the bits above). A block holds up to 900,000 bytes, so the table is up to 3.6 MB, larger than most cores' L2 cache.
- **The walk.** Start at the block's primary index. Each step loads the current row's entry, writes its byte, and takes the next row from the same entry. The next row is anywhere in the table, so the load usually misses the cache.
- **The wait.** The step after can't start until that load returns, because its address is in the load's result. A chain of dependent loads keeps one miss in flight, and the core idles through each one.

One courier. Each step (dark) is a few instructions; most of the time goes on waiting for the next address (light). Schematic, not to scale.

The walk was measured as latency-bound directly, on the machine where mibz2's prototype was built: walking 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 independent chains through one block, the cost fell from 28.5 to 4.4 cycles a byte of output ([compute frontier, section 2](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-27-compute-frontier.md#2-the-bz2-decode-phases-scaling-and-the-prototype>)). Memory bandwidth was nowhere near its limit. The walk was waiting, not moving data. libbzip2 and lbzip2 walk the one chain.

## 32 couriers, 32 independent journeys

Give each of 32 couriers a different delivery chain. While courier 1 waits for its next address, couriers 2, 3, 4… make progress. That is memory-level parallelism: the couriers don't travel faster, but there are enough independent journeys that waiting on one doesn't stop the rest. One courier is limited by the time it takes to get each new address; 32 keep many requests in flight.

Four of mibz2's 32 couriers. Each still waits as long for its address, but the waits overlap, and the core takes the other couriers' steps in the gaps. Schematic, not to scale.

> [!NOTE]
>
> **The correction that keeps the picture faithful**
>
> The CPU doesn't employ 32 workers, and the lanes aren't threads. **One core interleaves the instructions of 32 traversal chains**, and its out-of-order machinery overlaps their memory requests. The better image is one dispatch centre managing 32 motorcycles, each getting its next destination only when its last delivery returns an address.
>
> What counts is deliveries a second for the whole centre, not how fast one bike finishes its route: sustained throughput, not the latency of any one load. Every load still takes as long as before.
>
> Several threads are several dispatch centres, one a block: mibz2's workers decode whole blocks in parallel ([How it works](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/how-it-works/#threads>)). The lanes are the parallelism inside each one.

### Where the independent journeys come from

A block has one chain, not 32: the T-vector is a single cycle through every row (or, for a periodic text, a few). bzip2 carries no metadata to start a walk anywhere but the primary index. mibz2 makes the journeys itself:

- **Random starts.** 511 pseudo-random rows, plus the walk's own first row, become segment starts. A random row is a random position in the text, so the cycle is cut into 512 segments of about equal length. (Evenly spaced rows clustered in the text and stalled the lanes.)
- **Flagged starts end a segment.** Each start is flagged in bit 31 of its own T-vector entry, which links never use. A lane that reads a flagged entry has run into the next segment's start: its segment ends there, recording which start it ran into, and the lane takes the next unwalked segment.
- **32 lanes walk in lockstep.** Each round, every lane takes one step, writing its byte into its own segment's buffer.
- **The segments are stitched together afterwards.** From the first row's segment, each segment is followed by the one it ran into, until the block's length is reached. The output is exactly the plain walk's, byte for byte, including a periodic block's several cycles. The flags are cleared before the walk returns.
- **Short blocks walk plainly.** Under 64 KiB, the segments' bookkeeping costs more than the waits it hides; only a stream's last block is ever that short.

One chain cut at flagged starts into segments, walked by four lanes in whatever order the lanes take them, then joined in order. mibz2 cuts each block into 512 segments for 32 lanes.

### Prefetching: phoning ahead

Lanes alone weren't enough. Without help, a lane's next load is issued only when its instructions enter the core's reorder buffer, which is full of the other lanes' steps. So the misses in flight were bounded by how many steps that window holds, and adding lanes didn't add misses.

mibz2 issues a software prefetch of each lane's next entry as soon as its row is known (`prefetcht0` on x86-64, `prfm pldl1keep` on aarch64). A prefetch retires without waiting for its data, so every lane's miss starts at once. In the picture, the dispatcher phones each request through the moment an address is read, rather than when that courier's turn comes round on the board.

Try the counts yourself in this schematic. It has one dispatcher, whose paperwork for a step takes a tick or two, and each address takes 31 ticks to come back. The timings are made up for the picture.

The schematic needs JavaScript.

## The dispatcher becomes the bottleneck

There is only so much road, and one dispatcher. Add enough couriers and every wait is covered. Then the limit is the dispatcher: each step's paperwork, done for each courier in turn. Add more couriers past that point and the dispatcher spends more on coordination than the extra journeys earn.

In the core, the dispatcher's limits are these:

- **Instructions a step.** Every lane's step is a handful of instructions: the load, the flag test, the byte's store, the write pointer's advance, the buffer-end check, the prefetch. With the misses overlapped, the walk runs at the rate the core can issue those instructions.
- **Register pressure.** One lane's state (its row, its write pointers, its segment) fits in registers, but 32 lanes' state doesn't. It lives in the L1 cache, and every step loads and stores some of it.
- **Cache contention.** The lanes' table lines, the 512 segments' buffers and the lanes' own state share the same caches. At four threads, four walks share the L3.
- **Outstanding misses.** A core tracks only so many misses at once (its line fill buffers, and the L2's own queue). Beyond that, more lanes only queue.

The record shows both sides. Without the prefetch, 16 lanes were within noise of 12, and 24 or 32 were slower ([PR \#21](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/21>)). With it, 16 to 32 lanes were about 26–28% faster than 12 lanes without it, and within noise of each other at one walk. With four walks at once, 32 lanes won clearly. So mibz2 runs 32 lanes and 512 segments ([the measured points](<#lane-counts>)).

It also explains why a cleverer-looking algorithm can lose. Once 32 misses are in flight, **the walk is bound by instructions a step**, not by the latency of each load. A change that saves steps but makes each one dearer loses. A change that keeps the steps and makes them cheaper wins.

## Make the dispatcher efficient

Once there are enough couriers, cut the paperwork a step. That's how the walk got faster:

- **The flagged walk** ([\#12](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/12>)). It replaced the first segmented walk, which tested every step's row against a separate bitmap of the starts (12 lanes, 256 segments). The flag moved into the entry the step loads anyway, bytes went out through raw per-lane pointers instead of a growable vector's push, and the test for idle lanes left the hot loop.
- **The prefetch, with 32 lanes and 512 segments** ([\#21](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/21>)): every lane's next miss starts at once, as [above](<#prefetch>).
- **The shared-offset walk, after libsais's chain decode** ([\#37](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/37>), the default walk since 0.1.5). libsais 2.12's `decode_chains` runs `room` rounds of every chain at a shared output offset, where `room` is the fewest bytes any chain's buffer has spare. Within a pass, a lane's byte goes to its buffer's base plus the pass's offset, so the per-step pointer store and buffer-end test are gone. The lanes, the prefetch and the segments are unchanged, so the same misses are in flight. Only the instructions a step drop: one dispatcher's paperwork, done in batches.

Two cleverer-looking ideas from the literature were built, measured and dropped. Both changed the journeys themselves, and both lost to their extra cost a step:

- **The pair walk, ψ²** ([\#34](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/34>), after libsais and Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's super-alphabet). Each entry holds the row two steps on, so the walk takes half the steps, two bytes at each. But each step costs about twice as much: the second byte comes from a first-byte lookup. With the prefetch keeping 32 misses in flight, halving the dependent loads bought almost nothing, and the pair table took about three times as long to build. Envelopes holding two addresses mean fewer stops, but twice the paperwork at each, and the envelopes take three times as long to fill.
- **Precopy** ([\#36](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/36>), after Kärkkäinen and Puglisi). Where a stretch of the walk repeats one already walked, its bytes are copied instead of walked. It copied 31.5% of the Wikidata blocks' bytes, and was slower all the same. The repeat check ran on every step, and the steps it skipped were the cheap ones, whose table lines were already in cache. The cost is in the scattered steps, which repeats never cover. A courier who checks the logbook for a repeated stretch at every stop loses more time than the short, nearby stretches it saves.

The core's time once enough misses are in flight, schematically: the bytes out in the same time. The shared-offset walk keeps the journeys and cuts the bookkeeping. The pair walk halves the steps but doubles each one's work, and pays again in its build. Precopy adds a check to every step to skip a few cheap ones.

## The measurements

> [!WARNING]
>
> **Read these as indicative**
>
> These are the walk alone, on one thread, mostly on shared development machines. Each comparison holds only within its own row: the rows differ in machine, clock, corpus and repeats. The implementations differ in more than their lane count, too: the bitmap or the flag, the vector push or the raw pointers, the prefetch, and the segment count. Only the CI benchmark decides what merges.

### The walk alone

Cycles a byte of output (c/B), the walk on its own, one thread:

| change | before → after | where measured | source |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| the plain walk → the first segmented walk (12 lanes, a bitmap of the starts) | 31.4 → 14.1 | the prototype, `kernels/bz2k`: the wikidata-pq bench slice, a Xeon VM at 2.1 GHz | [compute frontier, section 2](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-27-compute-frontier.md#2-the-bz2-decode-phases-scaling-and-the-prototype>) |
| the bitmap walk → the flagged walk (both 12 lanes) | 31.8 → 17.2 | `examples/phases`: 13 MB of Wikidata dump blocks, a shared VM, at a nominal 2.8 GHz | [PR \#12](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/12>) |
| the flagged walk at 12 lanes → 32 lanes, 512 segments and the prefetch | 21.20 → 12.28 (four walks at once: 50.99 → 20.35) | the walk alone: the 431 Wikidata blocks, best of 5, a shared VM, at a nominal 2.8 GHz | [PR \#21](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/21>) |
| the flagged walk (32 lanes, the prefetch), in a whole decode's stage split | 11.90, 53.4% of a 22.31 c/B decode | `examples/phases`: the 431 Wikidata blocks, best of 3, at a nominal 2.8 GHz | [research synthesis](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-27-research-synthesis.md#the-bottleneck-the-leads-are-measured-against>) |
| the flagged walk on CI's runner | 6.96 and 7.33 (medians: the base and head of a change that left the walk alone), 60.3% of a decode | CI's per-stage table: `examples/phases` on the Wikidata blocks, 5 rounds, an EPYC 9V45 at 4.5 GHz | [PR \#35's bench](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/35#issuecomment-6448968226>) |
| the flagged walk → the shared-offset walk | 8.30 → 7.37 | the walk alone: Wikidata blocks, best of 5 a block, the shared machine | [PR \#37](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/37>) |
| unjoined chains, 1 → 16 (no segments, no join: a ceiling, not a decoder) | 28.5 → 4.4 | the prototype's latency test, as the first row | [compute frontier, section 2](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-27-compute-frontier.md#2-the-bz2-decode-phases-scaling-and-the-prototype>) |

The losing ideas, the walk alone on the shared machine: the pair walk's walk was about 10 c/B against the flagged walk's 10.4–10.8, but its build was 7.1–7.6 against 2.5 ([pair walk journal](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/journal/2026-10-27-pair-walk.md>)); Precopy was 13.5 against 10.3 c/B on Wikidata, with 31.5% of the bytes copied ([PR \#36](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/36>)).

### By lane count: the measured points

Only measured points are drawn, each chart on its own axes and naming its source: two sweeps so far, on different machines, corpora and walks, not to be read against each other. A finer sweep of lanes and prefetching is planned. Its points will go into [`assets/data/lane-sweeps.json`](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/master/docs/site/assets/data/lane-sweeps.json>), one panel a sweep, and appear here.

Loading the measured sweeps…

### The whole decoder, on CI

The walk is about 53–60% of a decode, so a walk change moves the whole decoder by less. Whole-decoder figures come only from the CI benchmark: paired rounds of a pull request's head against its base on one runner ([methodology](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/index.md>)). The walk's changes, on the Wikidata blocks (wall time, head over base, with its 95% interval; − is faster):

| change | 1 thread | 4 threads | bench |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| the flagged walk (\#12) | −10.7% (−11.3%, −10.2%) | −16.6% (−18.2%, −15.0%) | [\#12](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/12#issuecomment-6441420139>) |
| 32 lanes, 512 segments, the prefetch (\#21) | −13.2% (−13.8%, −12.5%) | −8.3% (−11.5%, −5.0%) | [\#21](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/21#issuecomment-6443760336>) |
| the pair walk, ψ² (\#34, not merged) | \+40.6% (+40.1%, +41.1%) | \+24.3% (+22.8%, +25.8%) | [\#34](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/34#issuecomment-6448612473>) |
| Precopy (\#36, not merged) | \+18.0% (+15.9%, +20.1%) | \+6.0% (+5.0%, +6.9%) | [\#36](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/36#issuecomment-6449155064>) |
| the shared-offset walk (\#37) | −10.3% (−10.6%, −10.0%) | −9.1% (−12.2%, −5.9%) | [\#37](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/37>), its first run (EPYC 9V74); its last, on a Xeon 6973P-C: −5.8% (−7.3%, −4.2%) and −2.7% (−4.1%, −1.3%) |

Each row is its own runner and its own base, so the rows don't add up. Master's figures over its commits are on the [History](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/history/index.md>) page, and mibz2 beside the other bzip2 decoders on [Alternatives](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/benchmarks/alternatives/index.md>).

## The picture, term by term

| in the picture | in the decoder |
| --- | --- |
| a courier | a lane: one traversal chain, walking one segment at a time |
| a delivery address, read on arrival | the next row, in the entry the step just loaded |
| waiting for the address | a cache miss on the T-vector |
| a delivery chain | a segment, from a flagged start row to the next start |
| the dispatcher | one core's instruction stream, interleaving all the lanes' steps |
| the paperwork for each step | the instructions a step: the flag test, the byte's store, the pointer and buffer bookkeeping |
| phoning ahead | the software prefetch of each lane's next entry |
| the road, the board's size | the core's limits: outstanding misses (line fill buffers), the reorder window, the caches |
| deliveries a second for the centre | bytes of output a second: throughput, not one load's latency |
| several dispatch centres | worker threads, one block each |

# What is checked, and when

## Block CRCs, before the block's bytes

Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned. A block whose CRC does not match returns none of its bytes: the error comes instead. The bytes returned before an error are exactly the stream's up to the bad block.

## Stream CRCs, at the stream's end

Each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. The bytes of a stream's blocks are returned as each block is verified, before the stream's own CRC has been read. So a streaming caller has the whole stream verified only once a read reaches its end without an error: until then, what it has read is provisional.

In Python, `BZ2Reader.verified` turns true only when a read returns the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched.

## Where an error was found

An error says where decoding failed: in Rust `Error { kind, block, bit }`, in Python the `DecodeError` message. That is which block, and the bit it starts at. A damaged bit can be found later than where it lies, since the input is only known to be wrong once something it encodes fails a check.

The error kinds (`ErrorKind`):

- the input: `Empty`, `NotBz2`, `Truncated`, `TrailingData`;
- each of libbzip2's block checks: `BadBlockMagic`, `BadOrigPtr`, `NoSymbols`, `BadGroups`, `BadSelectors`, `BadSelector`, `BadCodeLength`, `BadHuffmanCode`, `SelectorOverrun`, `RunTooLong`, `BlockTooLong`, `RunUnfinished`;
- `BlockCrc` and `StreamCrc`, with the stored and computed values;
- this decoder's refusals: `Randomised`, `BlockTooLarge`;
- `Io` (from a `BzReader`'s source), `RangeOvershoot`, `Cancelled`, and `Internal` (a caught panic: a bug).

## What is decoded, and what is refused

The format is libbzip2 1.0.8's, with every check it makes: bzip2 1.0 and later output. Four choices differ from it, and each has its own error:

| input | libbzip2 | mibz2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| randomised blocks (written only by bzip2 0.9.0 and earlier, before 1999) | decoded | refused (`Randomised`) |
| bytes after the last stream that do not begin another stream | ignored | an error (`TrailingData`): nothing after a stream is silently dropped |
| an oversubscribed Huffman code pointing past the alphabet | a stale table entry read | an error |
| a block whose compressed form passes 64 MiB (a real block is at most about 4.2 MB) | decoded | an error (`BlockTooLarge`) |

# How it works

## Threads

- **The scanner.** One thread reads each block's header and Huffman-coded symbols in order. This is the one sequential phase: a block's end is known only once its symbols are read. It finds blocks exactly, not by searching for the block magic, so a magic inside a block's data is never taken for a block. It is roughly a tenth of a decode on well-compressed text, more on poorly compressible data.
- **The workers.** Each worker finishes a block: move-to-front, the T-vector, the inverse BWT walk, RLE1 and the CRC.
- **The reader** takes the blocks in order. A block's error reaches the reader only once every block before it has been read.
- **Memory is bounded:** at most `slots` blocks are in flight (by default twice the threads), and the buffers are reused from block to block.

With one thread, the same phases run in order on the calling thread.

## The walk

The inverse BWT is a chain of dependent loads: each step's row is the previous step's load. A plain walk keeps one load in flight. The default walk (`bwt::walk_segments_room`, the flagged walk in passes) keeps many, one a lane ([Why 32 couriers beat one](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/couriers/index.md>) explains why, and where it stops paying):

- 512 pseudo-random rows, the walk's first among them, are segment starts;
- each start is flagged in its own T-vector entry, which ends the segment before it;
- 32 lanes walk segments in lockstep, each taking the next segment when its own ends, and each lane's next entry is prefetched as soon as its row is known;
- the lanes step in passes of `room` rounds, `room` the fewest bytes any lane's buffer has spare, each byte written at its lane's base plus the pass's offset, so a step has no pointer store or buffer-end test (after libsais's chain decode, [\#37](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/37>));
- the segments are joined in order.

It equals the plain walk on every list, lists of several cycles included: the join follows the segments' links until the block's length is reached. The flags are cleared before the walk returns. Blocks under 64 Ki are walked plainly. The kernel is behind `bwt::InverseBwt` (`Segmented`, the default; `Plain`), so a walk can be swapped and timed as part of the whole decoder.

## Kernels

`Kernels::detect()` chooses at run time: AVX2 (with BMI1) for move-to-front and RLE1, and PCLMULQDQ for the CRC. Each has a scalar twin, used on any other CPU and on aarch64 (`Kernels::scalar()`). The walk's gain is scalar code, memory-level parallelism, so it holds on any CPU.

# Prior work

- **The format and its checks are libbzip2's** (Julian Seward, bzip2 1.0.8, `decompress.c`). mibz2 follows its decoding rules and makes each of its checks, in its terms. Its Huffman decode tables are built as `BZ2_hbCreateDecodeTables` builds them, so a stream libbzip2 refuses is refused here too. It is a separate implementation in Rust, not a port of libbzip2's code. The tests use libbzip2 itself (the `bzip2` crate's bundled 1.0.8) as the oracle.
- **Interleaving several traversals of one BWT inversion** on one thread, so that out-of-order execution keeps their loads in flight, is Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's idea: "Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion", DCC 2012, pp. 99–108.

  - They also use a super-alphabet (an LF² table: two characters a dependent lookup) and "Precopy" for repetitive data. Neither is used here: both were built in mibz2 and lost ([why](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/concepts/couriers/#cheaper-steps>)).
  - What is particular here is only how the traversals are found in an existing bzip2 file, which carries no metadata for them: the random starts, the flagged starts that end each segment, and the joining in order.
- **libsais** (Ilya Grebnov), 2.12's cyclic inverse BWT, "as used by bzip2": its `RUN_LANES` store, 16 equal last-column bytes linked at once, is in mibz2's T-vector build. Its chain decode's shared-offset passes are mibz2's walk since 0.1.5 ([\#37](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/37>)).
- **Block-parallel decoding** is lbzip2's (Mikołaj Izdebski) and pbzip2's approach.
- **pbz2** (Soof Golan) arrived independently at a segmented, multi-chain walk too; the bake-off that found it is in the [journals](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/background/journals/index.md>).

# Get started

# Installation

## Python

mibz2 needs Python 3.10 or later. It has no Python dependencies.

```sh
pip install mibz2
```

or with uv:

```sh
uv add mibz2
```

Wheels are built for Linux (x86-64, aarch64), macOS (x86-64, arm64) and Windows (x64). Each uses the stable ABI (abi3), so one wheel covers every Python version from 3.10.

## Rust

```sh
cargo add mibz2
```

The library depends on std only. Its minimum supported Rust version is 1.80. The `python` feature builds the Python extension module, and is only for maturin.

# Quickstart

## Python

Write a .bz2 file with the standard library's `bz2`, to have one to read:

```python
import bz2

with bz2.open("sample.bz2", "wb") as f:
    for i in range(10_000):
        f.write(f"line {i}\n".encode())
```

A whole file in memory, decoded on every CPU this process may use, or on one thread:

```pycon
>>> import mibz2
>>> compressed = open("sample.bz2", "rb").read()
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(compressed)
>>> data == bz2.decompress(compressed)
True
>>> mibz2.decompress(compressed, threads=1) == data
True
```

A file read as it is decoded: `open` takes a path or a binary file object, and returns a buffered binary file. Its `raw.verified` turns true once a read has reached the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched:

```pycon
>>> with mibz2.open("sample.bz2") as f:
...     first = f.readline()
...     before = f.raw.verified
...     rest = f.read()
...     after = f.raw.verified
>>> first, before, after
(b'line 0\n', False, True)
```

A bad input raises `mibz2.DecodeError`, a `ValueError`, from `decompress` or from the read at which it is found. The message says which block and bit decoding failed at:

```pycon
>>> damaged = bytearray(compressed)
>>> damaged[len(damaged) // 2] ^= 0x10
>>> try:
...     mibz2.decompress(bytes(damaged))
... except mibz2.DecodeError as e:
...     print(type(e).__name__, isinstance(e, ValueError))
DecodeError True
```

## Rust

```rust
use std::io::Read;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // a whole .bz2 in memory (its streams one after another): on this thread, or on 4
    let data = std::fs::read("file.bz2")?;
    let text = mibz2::decode(&data)?;
    let same = mibz2::decode_parallel(&data, 4)?;
    assert_eq!(text, same);

    // any Read, as a Read: on this thread, or block-parallel on 4 worker threads
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    mibz2::BzReader::parallel(std::fs::File::open("file.bz2")?, 4).read_to_end(&mut out)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

A bad stream is an `mibz2::Error` (its `kind`, `block` and `bit`), or from a `BzReader` an `io::Error` of kind `InvalidData` wrapping it. The [Rust reference](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/reference/rust/index.md>) lists the rest: the push decoder, the block scanner and the decoding of a range of blocks.

# Blog

What mibz2's experiments are finding, and where they go next. The evidence behind each post is in the [journals](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/background/journals/index.md>) and the pull requests they link.

[mibz2 · Research blog](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/blog/index.md>)

# A faster table builder made the decoder slower: what the failure found in the walk

A builder that ran 20% fewer instructions made the whole bzip2 decoder 7–19% slower. Counting the whole decoder instead found the work in the walk, where an unbuilt design from our own record removed a third of it.

4 November 2026 · 10 min read · [Research in progress](<#6-what-is-still-open>)

[The last post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/blog/2026-11-04-compact30-constructor/index.md>) described a builder for compact30, a smaller table for undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform: about 2.1 MB per block where the production decoder's table takes 3.6 MB. Its inner loop fell from 49 instructions to 12, and across our reference corpus it built the table with about a fifth fewer instructions than the builder it replaced.

This post is about what happened when we put it into the production decoder. The decoder got slower. Understanding why led to a change in the production decoder itself, one that leaves its table exactly as it was and removes a fifth of the instructions it spends on each block.

## 1\. Three phases, one budget

After its Huffman and move-to-front stages, `mibz2` turns each bzip2 block back into bytes in three steps:

1. **Build** a navigation table from the block's transformed bytes: for each row, which row comes next, and which byte to emit.
2. **Walk** the table. Starting from a known row, follow the links, writing one byte per step. The decoder runs 32 independent walks ("lanes") at once, each through its own segment of the block, so that while one lane waits for memory the others keep going ([32 lanes, 8.6 chains](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/blog/2026-10-31-room-walk-overlap/index.md>)).
3. **The rest:** undo bzip2's run-length coding, check the CRC, and assemble the segments.

Here is where the instructions go on one full Wikidata block of 899,971 bytes, counted with Callgrind on production `decode_block`:

| Phase | Instructions | Share |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Build | 5,429,062 | 21% |
| Walk | 15,426,892 | 60% |
| The rest | 4,895,842 | 19% |
| **Whole block** | **25,751,796** |  |

The compact30 work had spent a week on the first row. The walk, three times as large, had been treated as settled.

## 2\. The port

The research builder went into production as the default kernel (\[PR

# 155\](https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/155)), with the production table kept as a fallback.

On the same block:

| Phase | Production | compact30 | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Build | 5,429,062 | 4,369,204 | −1,059,858 (−19.5%) |
| Walk | 15,426,892 | 20,207,700 | **\+4,780,808 (+31.0%)** |
| The rest | 4,895,842 | 4,953,557 | \+57,715 |
| **Whole block** | **25,751,796** | **29,530,461** | **\+3,778,665 (+14.7%)** |

The builder's saving survived the port. But the walk over the smaller table costs about 5.3 more instructions for every byte it writes, and that is more than the builder saves.

The reason is in the table's shape. A production entry is one 32-bit word holding both the next row and the byte, so a step is one load. compact30 packs 30 rows into a 64-byte record: a 16-bit offset per row and a 32-bit header shared by the group, holding the group's base row and its byte. A step therefore loads the offset, works out which group the row is in, loads the header, and adds. The table is smaller because each step does more.

The continuous-integration benchmark ran both builds on the same runner, paired over ten rounds. The compact30 decoder was 18.7% slower at one thread, 11.0% at two and 7.3% at four, with every interval excluding no change. CPU per byte rose about 18% at one thread, close to the 14.7% rise in instructions, so a smaller table bought no net speed on that machine. The PR was closed unmerged ([the write-up](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/8abefea4/docs/journal/2026-11-04-compact30-production-port.md>)).

Two things had made it look worthwhile. On our shared development machine it ran 3–4% faster, with intervals clear of zero. A smaller table fitting better in cache was a plausible explanation, and it didn't hold on the machine that decides. And the research gate counted the builder's instructions only, against a research baseline rather than production. Both are now fixed in the project's rules: every candidate is counted across the whole decoder against production before it goes near a pull request, and local timing is never the reason to open one.

## 3\. Looking at the walk itself

If the walk is three-fifths of the work, the question is no longer how to build a table more cheaply. It is what the production walk spends on each step. That question was already in our own record. [32 lanes, 8.6 chains](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/blog/2026-10-31-room-walk-overlap/index.md>) had proposed "Path B": the walk already overlaps its memory lookups well enough, so spend fewer instructions on each step and keep all 32 chains. A read-only analysis from 30 October, B2 (linked below), had gone further. It counted the shipped loop at 14.8 operations per byte, designed a kernel B ("the same 32 scalar chains with deferred flags and tiled commits") at 8–9, and fitted a model predicting what B would buy on each of CI's processors. Nobody had built it.

We came to it from the profiles, and only then recognised it as B. Here is what the profiles showed.

Callgrind can count every instruction separately. Here is the production walk's hot loop, as the compiler emitted it, with the count of each instruction on that block:

```text
  841,989  lea    r10,[r8+0x1]                 ; loop control
  841,989  mov    ebx,DWORD PTR [r11]          ; the lane's row, from memory
  841,989  mov    eax,DWORD PTR [r15+rbx*4]    ; T[row]: the lookup
  841,989  test   eax,eax                      ; does a segment start here?
  841,989  js     ...                          ;   (rarely)
  841,509  mov    edi,eax
  841,509  shr    edi,0x8                      ; the next row
  841,509  mov    DWORD PTR [r11],edi          ; the lane's row, back to memory
  841,509  prefetcht0 BYTE PTR [r15+rdi*4]     ; ask for the next lookup early
  841,509  mov    rdi,QWORD PTR [rsp+r8*8+0x70]; this lane's output pointer
  841,509  mov    BYTE PTR [rdi+rcx*1],al      ; the byte
  841,509  lea    rax,[r10-0x1]                ; loop control
  841,509  add    r11,0x20                     ; loop control
  841,509  mov    r8,r10                       ; loop control
  841,509  cmp    rax,0x1f                     ; loop control
  841,509  jb     ...                          ; loop control
```

That is sixteen instructions per step. About half of them do the decoding: read the lane's row, look it up, test for a segment boundary, shift out the next row, prefetch, store the byte. Most of the rest is the loop over the 32 lanes. The source says `for k in 0..32`, a fixed count, and the compiler kept it as a counted loop instead of unrolling it.

It kept it rolled because of what sits inside the loop. When a lane reaches the end of its segment, it hands that segment over and takes the next one from a queue. That handover is rare (about 0.06% of steps) but large, and having it inside the loop body keeps the loop too big to unroll.

## 4\. Taking the handover out

The change has three parts ([PR \#157](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/157>)).

**Step, then hand over.** Each round, every lane whose entry doesn't start a new segment takes its step. A lane whose entry does is only marked, as a bit in a 64-bit mask. Once every lane has stepped, the marked lanes are handed over in lane order.

This reorders work, so it has to be shown not to change the output. A step reads the table, which nothing in the walk writes, and writes only the lane's own row and a byte in that lane's own buffer. A handover changes only its own lane, the segment it finishes, the segment it takes and the queue's position. So every step commutes with every other lane's handover, and the handovers still run in lane order. The segments are taken in the same order, and every byte lands where it did before.

The one delicate case is the queue running out partway through a round. The walk then leaves the round for a slower tail loop, and the two orders can leave a later lane in different states. In the old order it hasn't stepped yet. In the new one it has. The tail would take that same step first, so the buffers end up the same, but the states in between are not. The argument is a simulation relation over commuting steps, not equality of state. (Our Researcher agent made that correction, and asked for tests that tell the two apart.)

**Unroll by hand.** Splitting the loop alone did nothing: the compiler still emitted the same sixteen instructions. So the step is written out eight times per iteration, with a remainder loop for lane counts that aren't a multiple of eight.

**Store before shifting.** The byte is the entry's low eight bits, and the next row is the entry shifted right by eight. Storing the byte first lets the shift happen in place, which saves a register copy.

A step is now nine instructions, plus about half an instruction of loop control:

| Block | Production | This change | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 (899,971 B) | 25,751,796 | 20,184,697 | −21.6% |
| 41 (900,000 B) | 25,168,380 | 19,480,512 | −22.6% |
| 233 (899,978 B) | 25,588,404 | 19,989,537 | −21.9% |
| 400 (899,993 B) | 25,129,254 | 19,490,536 | −22.4% |

The build and the rest are identical to the instruction. The whole difference is the walk, which fell by 36% including its setup, handovers and tail. Small blocks take a simpler walk and don't change. Output is identical on every block, and the tests include one built for this change. It drives the walk through random columns until every new interleaving has occurred: several lanes reaching segment ends in the same round, and the queue running out with marked lanes still waiting, after a handover, and with a later lane already stepped onto its own segment's end. It fails if the offsets the tail picks up from are changed.

That is kernel B, nine instructions a step against B2's predicted eight to nine. It is as large a cut in whole-decoder instructions as anything the campaign has found. It leaves the table as it was, so it composes with whatever else is done to the walk.

## 5\. Instructions are not time, and the model was wrong about how much

The continuous-integration benchmark measured it twice, on the same walk machine code, landing on two different processors. The Wikidata corpus, paired over ten rounds each:

| Threads | EPYC 9V45, wall | EPYC 7763, wall |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | −4.2% (−8.0%, −0.3%) | −2.4% (−3.6%, −1.2%) |
| 2 | \+2.2% (−0.6%, +5.1%) | −4.9% (−9.5%, −0.1%) |
| 4 | \+0.4% (−2.8%, +3.8%) | \+0.2% (−2.1%, +2.7%) |

At one thread it is faster on both. With more threads, the picture depends on the machine.

On the 7763 the benchmark also times each stage on one thread. The walk went from 4.04 to 3.78 cycles per byte, a ratio of 0.925 (0.856 to 0.999). A 36% cut in instructions bought 7.5% of the walk's time.

B2 had predicted much more. Its best-supported model gives a step's time as its issue time plus a miss penalty limited by the processor's window: w = U/D + ℓ·U/R. For the 7763 it predicted B's walk at 0.73 to 0.76 of A's, and −10% to −11% of decoder time. The measurement lies outside that range. So does the reading in which the walk is limited purely by its instruction rate (0.55 to 0.65). What it doesn't exclude is the remaining hypothesis B2 listed: the walk is capped by how many outstanding misses one core can track, so fewer instructions per step can't make it much faster (0.95 or more).

That is a useful negative result. It says the walk on this machine is close to limited by its memory requests, not its instructions. The next large gains would then have to come from fewer misses per byte, not fewer instructions per step.

## 6\. What is still open

**Shipping.** The change met the merge gate. The one-thread gain was confirmed on two processors, with nothing regressing beyond a small, unreplicated slip on one synthetic corpus. It is now on master, unreleased.

**Why B2's model overestimated.** Either the miss term isn't ℓ·U/R as fitted, or the latency of each miss rises when more are in flight, as B2's own risks list. B puts more misses in flight than A. A refit to A and B together, which can now both be measured, should say which term has to move.

**Why the multi-thread result depends on the machine.** On the 9V45, two threads lost the gain; on the 7763 they kept it. There are several candidates: - **A shared bottleneck.** Something shared across copies may bind. - **The run's shape.** The benchmark's two-thread run puts four threads (two workers, the scanner and the reader) on two CPUs. - **Interference.** It may be the effect [Investigating inverse-BWT memory interference](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/blog/2026-11-01-inverse-bwt-memory-interference/index.md>) measured on a four-core machine. That post proposed causes and tests, but didn't settle the cause. CI's four-thread runs are two cores with SMT, not four cores.

The cheapest decisive experiment is the falsifier B2 described: time the walk alone, A against B, at one copy, two copies on separate cores, and on the two siblings of one core, on each machine.

**The other walks.** The cooperative walk, used on machines with many cores, and the flagged walk carry the same rolled loop. Whether to port the change waits on that experiment.

The lesson is about memory as much as measurement. A faster builder made the decoder slower because nobody had counted the walk. Counting it found a change our own analysis had designed and priced, and then left unbuilt. Building it tested the analysis, and part of it failed. The project's record is now treated as working memory: every new direction starts from what earlier analyses proposed, measured or left untested.

---

**Research records:** [The port, PR \#155](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/155>) · [Its write-up](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/8abefea4/docs/journal/2026-11-04-compact30-production-port.md>) · [Its profiles](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/c493a45d/docs/journal/compact30-channel/evidence/port-b4786f66>) · [The walk change, PR \#157](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/157>) · [Its profiles, listings and tests](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/tree/b0f6e89d/docs/journal/compact30-channel/evidence/walk-75b13f00>) · [B2, the gathered walk: the model and kernel B](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/9723f068/docs/journal/2026-10-30-b2-gathered-walk.md>) · [The research register](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/4dac7abc/docs/journal/2026-10-30-research-portfolio-register.md>) · [Whole-decoder accounting, charter §5.6](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/45e6cfeb/docs/journal/2026-11-04-compact30-research-charter.md>)

[mibz2 · Research blog](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/blog/index.md>)

# Call on mibz2: cutting instructions from bzip2 decoding with an autonomous swarm

Each of four agents does one part of the research. A GitHub doorbell lets them hand work to each other directly, without me acting as their message bus.

4 November 2026 · 10 min read · [Meta](<#8-where-it-stands>)

[The last post](<https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/pr-preview/pr-158/blog/2026-11-04-compact30-constructor/index.md>) was about compact30, my effort to give the decoder's navigation table a smaller representation. Four agents did the research behind it, but until today they could only work together if I copied each one's messages to the next by hand.

This post is about how they now pass work between themselves through the repository: who does what, how a message gets from one agent to another, and what I learnt from an afternoon of running it. It covers the setup and its first full cycle. Whether it actually makes the research faster, we'll have to wait and see.

## 1\. A tale of four agents

The Coordinator is Claude Code. It writes the code for each change in the plan, compiles it, runs the tests and keeps the results. When a result is ready it posts a checkpoint: a comment saying what was built and which commit holds the evidence.

The Guardian and the Researcher both read every checkpoint, looking for different things. The Guardian checks the result against the research charter: which gates it passes, what work can follow, and what has to come to me. The Researcher looks at the reasoning: whether the argument holds, whether something else explains the numbers, whether there's a better direction, and whether the Guardian has got it right.

The Optimiser works on the instruction counts themselves. It reads the source, the compiled listings and the execution counts, works out transformations that remove instructions, and keeps the ledger of what each one saves. Its proposals are what the Coordinator builds next.

The Guardian, the Researcher and the Optimiser all run Astra, a model I use through ChatGPT, each as a ChatGPT Work task with its own reasoning-effort setting. What separates them is what they're responsible for, not the model. The roles, and the branch each one owns, are written down in [ROLES.md](<https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/blob/09e4ef6cb7c845781b0a2cb0d2c1a4fe6f33fe47/docs/journal/compact30-channel/ROLES.md>). To reproduce the setup, these are the settings:

| Role | Runs as | Model | Reasoning effort | Started by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinator | Claude Code session | Claude, as configured for the session | High | a subscription to the PRs it follows |
| Guardian | ChatGPT Work task, *Compact30 (W) Guardian* | Astra | Extra High | any PR comment; acts only on a `CHECKPOINT` |
| Optimiser | ChatGPT Work task, *Compact30 (W) Optimiser* | Astra | Ultra | any PR comment; acts only on a `CHECKPOINT` addressed to it |
| Researcher | ChatGPT Work task, *Compact30 (W) Researcher* | Astra | Extra High | any PR comment; acts only on a message addressed to it |

The team: three Astra agents and Claude Code, joined by one repository

Claude Code builds each change and posts a checkpoint. The Guardian checks it against the rules and the Researcher checks the reasoning, while the Optimiser hunts for more instructions to cut. All four work through the same repository.

## 2\. Every result is a commit

A checkpoint points at a commit, never at a branch, because a branch keeps moving. The commit holds the source and its baseline, the compiled listings, the toolchain, the test records, the execution counts and the arithmetic that ties them together. Reports and scripts go in files, and the comment links to them.

That lets a reader check a claim rather than take it on trust. If the Optimiser predicts that a change will remove a load from the inner loop, the checkpoint shows whether the compiled code actually lost it, whether setup got more expensive, whether a caller picked up a spill, and how often each path runs.

Each agent writes only to its own branch: the Coordinator to the implementation branches, the others to their reports, decision logs and ledgers. Every file has one author, and a review never edits the code it reviews. Each agent also keeps its working state on its branch, which is why a fresh run can pick up exactly where the last one stopped.

## 3\. Comments as messages, events as the clock

The agents talk in comments on pull requests. Each comment starts with a short header:

